00011| Welcome to the Next.js documentation!
00012| 
00013| ## What is Next.js?
00014| 
00015| Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.
00016| 
00017| It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.
00018| 
00019| Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.
00020| 
00021| ## How to use the docs
00022| 
00023| The docs are organized into 3 sections:
00024| 
00025| - [Getting Started](/docs/app/getting-started): Step-by-step tutorials to help you create a new application and learn the core Next.js features.
00026| - [Guides](/docs/app/guides): Tutorials on specific use cases, choose what's relevant to you.
00027| - [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference): Detailed technical reference for every feature.
00028| 
00029| Use the sidebar to navigate through the sections, or search (`Ctrl+K` or `Cmd+K`) to quickly find a page.
00030| 
00031| ## App Router and Pages Router
00032| 
00033| Next.js has two different routers:
00034| 
00035| - **App Router**: The newer router that supports new React features like Server Components.
00036| - **Pages Router**: The original router, still supported and being improved.
00037| 
00038| At the top of the sidebar, you'll notice a dropdown menu that allows you to switch between the [App Router](/docs/app) and the [Pages Router](/docs/pages) docs.
00039| 
00040| ### React version handling
00041| 
00042| The App Router and Pages Router handle React versions differently:
00043| 
00044| - **App Router**: Uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries) built-in, which include all the stable React 19 changes, as well as newer features being validated in frameworks, prior to a new React release.
00045| 
00046| - **Pages Router**: Uses the React version installed in your project's `package.json`.
00047| 
00048| This approach ensures new React features work reliably in the App Router while maintaining backwards compatibility for existing Pages Router applications.
00049| 
00050| ## Pre-requisite knowledge
00051| 
00052| Our documentation assumes some familiarity with web development. Before getting started, it'll help if you're comfortable with:
00053| 
00054| - HTML
00055| - CSS
00056| - JavaScript
00057| - React
00058| 
00059| If you're new to React or need a refresher, we recommend starting with our [React Foundations course](/learn/react-foundations), and the [Next.js Foundations course](/learn/dashboard-app) that has you building an application as you learn.
00060| 
00061| ## Accessibility
00062| 
00063| For the best experience when using a screen reader, we recommend using Firefox and NVDA, or Safari and VoiceOver.
00064| 
00065| ## Join our Community
00066| 
00067| If you have questions about anything related to Next.js, you're always welcome to ask our community on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions), [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/bUG2bvbtHy), [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/nextjs), and [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/nextjs).
00068|

Welcome to the Next.js documentation!

## What is Next.js?

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.

It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.

Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

This guide walks through understanding instant navigations, writing a route that navigates instantly, visualizing what's in the initial UI, and locking the behavior in with end-to-end tests.

## What "instant" means

A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks.

---
title: Ensuring instant navigations
description: Learn how to structure your app to prefetch and prerender more content, providing instant page loads and client navigations.
nav_title: Instant navigation
related:
  title: Learn more
  description: Explore the full instant API, caching, and revalidation.
  links:
    - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant

    - app/getting-started/caching
    - app/getting-started/revalidating
    - app/guides/prefetching
---

This guide walks through understanding instant navigations, writing a route that navigates instantly, visualizing what's in the initial UI, and locking the behavior in with end-to-end tests.

## What "instant" means

A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks.

00230| ### `scroll`
00231| 
00232| **Defaults to `true`.** The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport. However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element.
00233| 
00234| When `scroll = {false}`, Next.js will not attempt to scroll to the first Page element.
00235| 
00236| > **Good to know**: Next.js checks if `scroll: false` before managing scroll behavior. If scrolling is enabled, it identifies the relevant DOM node for navigation and inspects each top-level element. All non-scrollable elements and those without rendered HTML are bypassed, this includes sticky or fixed positioned elements, and non-visible elements such as those calculated with `getBoundingClientRect`. Next.js then continues through siblings until it identifies a scrollable element that is visible in the viewport.

00294| ### `prefetch`
00295| 
00296| <AppOnly>
00297| 
00298| Prefetching happens when a `<Link />` component enters the user's viewport (initially or through scroll). Next.js prefetches and loads the linked route (denoted by the `href`) and its data in the background to improve the performance of client-side navigations. If the prefetched data has expired by the time the user hovers over a `<Link />`, Next.js will attempt to prefetch it again. **Prefetching is only enabled in production**.
00299| 
00300| The following values can be passed to the `prefetch` prop:
00301| 
00302| - **`"auto"` or `null` (default)**: Prefetch behavior depends on whether the route is static or dynamic. For static routes, the full route will be prefetched (including all its data). For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading#instant-loading-states) boundary will be prefetched.
00303| - **`true`**: The full route is prefetched for both static and dynamic routes. With [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) enabled, the prefetch includes the [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) and cached content that depends on the link's URL data. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching).
00304| - `false`: Prefetching will never happen both on entering the viewport and on hover.
00305| 
00306| > **With Partial Prefetching enabled** ([`partialPrefetching: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching)): the default changes. `auto` prefetches the per-route [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) (the route's static and cached content) instead of the full page. See [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the full behavior change.
00307| 
00308| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00309| import Link from 'next/link'
00310| 
00311| export default function Page() {
00312|   return (
00313|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00314|       Dashboard
00315|     </Link>
00316|   )
00317| }
00318| ```
00319| 
00320| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00321| import Link from 'next/link'
00322| 
00323| export default function Page() {
00324|   return (
00325|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00326|       Dashboard
00327|     </Link>
00328|   )
00329| }
00330| ```
00331| 
00332| </AppOnly>

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.

00537| ## Examples

00542| 
00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher

00550| interface Post {
00551|   id: number
00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}
00564|     </ul>
00565|   )
00566| }
00567| ```

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers

00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

00230| ### `scroll`
00231| 
00232| **Defaults to `true`.** The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport. However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element.
00233| 
00234| When `scroll = {false}`, Next.js will not attempt to scroll to the first Page element.
00235| 
00236| > **Good to know**: Next.js checks if `scroll: false` before managing scroll behavior. If scrolling is enabled, it identifies the relevant DOM node for navigation and inspects each top-level element. All non-scrollable elements and those without rendered HTML are bypassed, this includes sticky or fixed positioned elements, and non-visible elements such as those calculated with `getBoundingClientRect`. Next.js then continues through siblings until it identifies a scrollable element that is visible in the viewport.
00237|

00247|     </Link>
00248|   )

00294| ### `prefetch`
00295| 
00296| <AppOnly>
00297| 
00298| Prefetching happens when a `<Link />` component enters the user's viewport (initially or through scroll). Next.js prefetches and loads the linked route (denoted by the `href`) and its data in the background to improve the performance of client-side navigations. If the prefetched data has expired by the time the user hovers over a `<Link />`, Next.js will attempt to prefetch it again. **Prefetching is only enabled in production**.
00299| 
00300| The following values can be passed to the `prefetch` prop:
00301| 
00302| - **`"auto"` or `null` (default)**: Prefetch behavior depends on whether the route is static or dynamic. For static routes, the full route will be prefetched (including all its data). For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading#instant-loading-states) boundary will be prefetched.
00303| - **`true`**: The full route is prefetched for both static and dynamic routes. With [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) enabled, the prefetch includes the [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) and cached content that depends on the link's URL data. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching).
00304| - `false`: Prefetching will never happen both on entering the viewport and on hover.
00305| 
00306| > **With Partial Prefetching enabled** ([`partialPrefetching: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching)): the default changes. `auto` prefetches the per-route [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) (the route's static and cached content) instead of the full page. See [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the full behavior change.
00307| 
00308| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00309| import Link from 'next/link'
00310| 
00311| export default function Page() {
00312|   return (
00313|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00314|       Dashboard
00315|     </Link>
00316|   )
00317| }
00318| ```
00319| 
00320| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00321| import Link from 'next/link'
00322| 
00323| export default function Page() {
00324|   return (
00325|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00326|       Dashboard
00327|     </Link>
00328|   )
00329| }
00330| ```
00331| 
00332| </AppOnly>
00333|

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.

00537| ## Examples
00538| 
00539| The following examples demonstrate how to use the `<Link>` component in different scenarios.

00541| <AppOnly>
00542| 
00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher
00548| import Link from 'next/link'
00549| 
00550| interface Post {
00551|   id: number
00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}
00564|     </ul>
00565|   )
00566| }
00567| ```
00568| 
00569| ```jsx filename="app/blog/post-list.js" switcher

00577|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00578|         </li>
00579|       ))}

00581|   )
00582| }
00583| ```

00787| ### Replace the URL instead of push
00788| 
00789| The default behavior of the `Link` component is to `push` a new URL into the `history` stack. You can use the `replace` prop to prevent adding a new entry, as in the following example:
00790| 
00791| <AppOnly>
00792| 
00793| ```tsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00794| import Link from 'next/link'
00795| 
00796| export default function Page() {
00797|   return (
00798|     <Link href="/about" replace>
00799|       About us
00800|     </Link>
00801|   )
00802| }

00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.

00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.

00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:

00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )

00956|         </header>

It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.

00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```

01093| 
01094| You can use the `onNavigate` prop to block navigation when certain conditions are met, such as when a form has unsaved changes. 00230| ### `scroll`
00231| 
00232| **Defaults to `true`.** The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport. However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element.
00233| 
00234| When `scroll = {false}`, Next.js will not attempt to scroll to the first Page element.
00235| 
00236| > **Good to know**: Next.js checks if `scroll: false` before managing scroll behavior. If scrolling is enabled, it identifies the relevant DOM node for navigation and inspects each top-level element. All non-scrollable elements and those without rendered HTML are bypassed, this includes sticky or fixed positioned elements, and non-visible elements such as those calculated with `getBoundingClientRect`. Next.js then continues through siblings until it identifies a scrollable element that is visible in the viewport.
00237|

00241| import Link from 'next/link'

00243| export default function Page() {

00245|     <Link href="/dashboard" scroll={false}>

00247|     </Link>
00248|   )
00249| }
00250| ```

00294| ### `prefetch`
00295| 
00296| <AppOnly>
00297| 
00298| Prefetching happens when a `<Link />` component enters the user's viewport (initially or through scroll). Next.js prefetches and loads the linked route (denoted by the `href`) and its data in the background to improve the performance of client-side navigations. If the prefetched data has expired by the time the user hovers over a `<Link />`, Next.js will attempt to prefetch it again. **Prefetching is only enabled in production**.
00299| 
00300| The following values can be passed to the `prefetch` prop:
00301| 
00302| - **`"auto"` or `null` (default)**: Prefetch behavior depends on whether the route is static or dynamic. For static routes, the full route will be prefetched (including all its data). For dynamic routes, the partial route down to the nearest segment with a [`loading.js`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading#instant-loading-states) boundary will be prefetched.
00303| - **`true`**: The full route is prefetched for both static and dynamic routes. With [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) enabled, the prefetch includes the [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) and cached content that depends on the link's URL data. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching).
00304| - `false`: Prefetching will never happen both on entering the viewport and on hover.
00305| 
00306| > **With Partial Prefetching enabled** ([`partialPrefetching: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/partialPrefetching)): the default changes. `auto` prefetches the per-route [App Shell](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) (the route's static and cached content) instead of the full page. See [Adopting Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching) for the full behavior change.
00307| 
00308| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00309| import Link from 'next/link'
00310| 
00311| export default function Page() {
00312|   return (
00313|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00314|       Dashboard
00315|     </Link>
00316|   )
00317| }
00318| ```
00319| 
00320| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00321| import Link from 'next/link'
00322| 
00323| export default function Page() {
00324|   return (
00325|     <Link href="/dashboard" prefetch={false}>
00326|       Dashboard
00327|     </Link>
00328|   )
00329| }
00330| ```
00331| 
00332| </AppOnly>
00333|

00453| ### `onNavigate`
00454| 
00455| An event handler called during client-side navigation. The handler receives an event object that includes a `preventDefault()` method, allowing you to cancel the navigation if needed.
00456| 
00457| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00458| import Link from 'next/link'
00459| 
00460| export default function Page() {
00461|   return (
00462|     <Link
00463|       href="/dashboard"
00464|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00465|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00466|         console.log('Navigating...')
00467| 
00468|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00469|         // e.preventDefault()
00470|       }}
00471|     >
00472|       Dashboard
00473|     </Link>
00474|   )
00475| }
00476| ```
00477| 
00478| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00479| import Link from 'next/link'
00480| 
00481| export default function Page() {
00482|   return (
00483|     <Link
00484|       href="/dashboard"
00485|       onNavigate={(e) => {
00486|         // Only executes during SPA navigation
00487|         console.log('Navigating...')
00488| 
00489|         // Optionally prevent navigation
00490|         // e.preventDefault()
00491|       }}
00492|     >
00493|       Dashboard
00494|     </Link>
00495|   )
00496| }
00497| ```
00498| 
00499| > **Good to know**: While `onClick` and `onNavigate` may seem similar, they serve different purposes. `onClick` executes for all click events, while `onNavigate` only runs during client-side navigation. Some key differences:
00500| >
00501| > - When using modifier keys (`Ctrl`/`Cmd` + Click), `onClick` executes but `onNavigate` doesn't since Next.js prevents default navigation for new tabs.
00502| > - External URLs won't trigger `onNavigate` since it's only for client-side and same-origin navigations.
00503| > - Links with the `download` attribute will work with `onClick` but not `onNavigate` since the browser will treat the linked URL as a download.
00504|

00537| ## Examples

00542| 
00543| ### Linking to dynamic route segments
00544| 
00545| When linking to [dynamic segments](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes), you can use [template literals and interpolation](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:
00546| 
00547| ```tsx filename="app/blog/post-list.tsx" switcher
00548| import Link from 'next/link'
00549| 
00550| interface Post {
00551|   id: number
00552|   title: string
00553|   slug: string
00554| }
00555| 
00556| export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
00557|   return (
00558|     <ul>
00559|       {posts.map((post) => (
00560|         <li key={post.id}>
00561|           <Link href={`/blog/${post.slug}`}>{post.title}</Link>
00562|         </li>
00563|       ))}
00564|     </ul>
00565|   )
00566| }
00567| ```

00687| ### Scrolling to an `id`

00763|           href={{
00764|             pathname: '/blog/[slug]',
00765|             query: { slug: 'my-post' },
00766|           }}
00767|         >
00768|           Blog Post
00769|         </Link>
00770|       </li>
00771|     </ul>
00772|   )
00773| }
00774| 
00775| export default Home
00776| ```
00777| 
00778| The above example has a link to:
00779| 
00780| - A predefined route: `/about?name=test`
00781| - A [dynamic route](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/dynamic-routes#convention): `/blog/my-post`
00782| 
00783| You can use every property as defined in the [Node.js URL module documentation](https://nodejs.org/api/url.html#url_url_strings_and_url_objects).
00784| 
00785| </PagesOnly>
00786| 
00787| ### Replace the URL instead of push
00788| 
00789| The default behavior of the `Link` component is to `push` a new URL into the `history` stack. You can use the `replace` prop to prevent adding a new entry, as in the following example:
00790| 
00791| <AppOnly>
00792| 
00793| ```tsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00794| import Link from 'next/link'
00795| 
00796| export default function Page() {
00797|   return (
00798|     <Link href="/about" replace>
00799|       About us
00800|     </Link>
00801|   )
00802| }
00803| ```
00804| 
00805| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00806| import Link from 'next/link'
00807| 
00808| export default function Page() {
00809|   return (
00810|     <Link href="/about" replace>
00811|       About us
00812|     </Link>
00813|   )
00814| }
00815| ```
00816| 
00817| </AppOnly>
00818| 
00819| <PagesOnly>
00820| 
00821| ```tsx filename="pages/index.js" switcher

00829|   )
00830| }

00832|

00844| 
00845| </PagesOnly>
00846| 
00847| ### Disable scrolling to the top of the page
00848| 
00849| <AppOnly>
00850| 
00851| The default scrolling behavior of `<Link>` in Next.js **is to maintain scroll position**, similar to how browsers handle back and forwards navigation. When you navigate to a new [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), scroll position will stay the same as long as the Page is visible in the viewport.
00852| 
00853| However, if the Page is not visible in the viewport, Next.js will scroll to the top of the first Page element. If you'd like to disable this behavior, you can pass `scroll={false}` to the `<Link>` component, or `scroll: false` to `router.push()` or `router.replace()`.
00854| 
00855| ```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
00856| import Link from 'next/link'
00857| 
00858| export default function Page() {
00859|   return (
00860|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00861|       Disables scrolling to the top
00862|     </Link>
00863|   )
00864| }
00865| ```
00866| 
00867| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
00868| import Link from 'next/link'
00869| 
00870| export default function Page() {
00871|   return (
00872|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00873|       Disables scrolling to the top
00874|     </Link>
00875|   )
00876| }
00877| ```
00878| 
00879| Using `router.push()` or `router.replace()`:
00880| 
00881| ```jsx
00882| // useRouter
00883| import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'
00884| 
00885| const router = useRouter()
00886| 
00887| router.push('/dashboard', { scroll: false })
00888| ```
00889| 
00890| </AppOnly>
00891| 
00892| <PagesOnly>
00893| 
00894| The default behavior of `Link` is to scroll to the top of the page. When there is a hash defined it will scroll to the specific id, like a normal `<a>` tag. To prevent scrolling to the top / hash `scroll={false}` can be added to `Link`:
00895| 
00896| ```jsx filename="pages/index.js" switcher
00897| import Link from 'next/link'
00898| 
00899| export default function Home() {
00900|   return (
00901|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00902|       Disables scrolling to the top
00903|     </Link>
00904|   )
00905| }
00906| ```
00907| 
00908| ```tsx filename="pages/index.tsx" switcher

00910| 
00911| export default function Home() {
00912|   return (
00913|     <Link href="/#hashid" scroll={false}>
00914|       Disables scrolling to the top
00915|     </Link>
00916|   )
00917| }
00918| ```
00919| 
00920| </PagesOnly>
00921| 
00922| ### Scroll offset with sticky headers
00923| 
00924| Because Next.js skips sticky and fixed positioned elements when finding the scroll target, content may end up behind a sticky header after navigation. For example, if your layout has a sticky header:
00925| 
00926| ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
00927| import './globals.css'
00928| 
00929| export default function RootLayout({
00930|   children,
00931| }: {
00932|   children: React.ReactNode
00933| }) {
00934|   return (
00935|     <html lang="en">
00936|       <body>
00937|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00938|           {/* Navigation */}
00939|         </header>
00940|         {children}
00941|       </body>
00942|     </html>
00943|   )
00944| }
00945| ```
00946| 
00947| ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher
00948| import './globals.css'
00949| 
00950| export default function RootLayout({ children }) {
00951|   return (
00952|     <html lang="en">
00953|       <body>
00954|         <header className="sticky top-0 h-16 bg-white">
00955|           {/* Navigation */}
00956|         </header>
00957|         {children}
00958|       </body>
00959|     </html>
00960|   )
00961| }
00962| ```
00963| 
00964| You can account for its height using [`scroll-padding-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-padding-top) on the scroll container:
00965| 
00966| ```css filename="app/globals.css"
00967| html {
00968|   scroll-padding-top: 64px; /* Match the height of your sticky header */
00969| }
00970| ```
00971| 
00972| This is a browser CSS property that offsets scroll-based positioning. It applies whenever Next.js uses the native [`scrollIntoView()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/scrollIntoView) API, including hash fragment (`#id`) navigation. Alternatively, you can use [`scroll-margin-top`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scroll-margin-top) on individual target elements instead of setting a global offset.
00973| 
00974| ### Prefetching links in Proxy
00975| 
00976| It's common to use [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) for authentication or other purposes that involve rewriting the user to a different page. In order for the `<Link />` component to properly prefetch links with rewrites via Proxy, you need to tell Next.js both the URL to display and the URL to prefetch. This is required to avoid un-necessary fetches to proxy to know the correct route to prefetch.
00977| 
00978| For example, if you want to serve a `/dashboard` route that has authenticated and visitor views, you can add the following in your Proxy to redirect the user to the correct page:
00979| 
00980| ```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
00981| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00982| 
00983| export function proxy(request: Request) {
00984|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
00985|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
00986|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
00987|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
00988|     } else {
00989|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
00990|     }
00991|   }
00992| }
00993| ```
00994| 
00995| ```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
00996| import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
00997| 
00998| export function proxy(request) {
00999|   const nextUrl = request.nextUrl
01000|   if (nextUrl.pathname === '/dashboard') {
01001|     if (request.cookies.authToken) {
01002|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/auth/dashboard', request.url))
01003|     } else {
01004|       return NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/public/dashboard', request.url))
01005|     }
01006|   }
01007| }
01008| ```
01009| 
01010| In this case, you would want to use the following code in your `<Link />` component:
01011| 
01012| <AppOnly>
01013| 
01014| ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
01015| 'use client'
01016| 
01017| import Link from 'next/link'
01018| import useIsAuthed from './hooks/useIsAuthed' // Your auth hook
01019| 
01020| export default function Page() {
01021|   const isAuthed = useIsAuthed()
01022|   const path = isAuthed ? '/auth/dashboard' : '/public/dashboard'
01023|   return (
01024|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01025|       Dashboard
01026|     </Link>
01027|   )
01028| }
01029| ```
01030| 
01031| ```js filename="app/page.js" switcher

01033|

01036|

01041|     <Link as="/dashboard" href={path}>
01042|       Dashboard
01043|     </Link>
01044|   )
01045| }
01046| ```
01047| 
01048| </AppOnly>
01049| 
01050| <PagesOnly>
01051| 
01052| ```tsx filename="pages/index.tsx" switcher

01054|

01068|

01086| > **Good to know**: If you're using [Dynamic Routes](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/dynamic-routes#convention), you'll need to adapt your `as` and `href` props. For example, if you have a Dynamic Route like `/dashboard/authed/[user]` that you want to present differently via proxy, you would write: `<Link href={{ pathname: '/dashboard/authed/[user]', query: { user: username } }} as="/dashboard/[user]">Profile</Link>`.

01088| </PagesOnly>
01089| 
01090| <AppOnly>
01091| 
01092| ### Blocking navigation
01093| 
01094| You can use the `onNavigate` prop to block navigation when certain conditions are met, such as when a form has unsaved changes. When you need to block navigation across multiple components in your app (like preventing navigation from any link while a form is being edited), React Context provides a clean way to share this blocking state. First, create a context to track the navigation blocking state:
01095| 
01096| ```tsx filename="app/contexts/navigation-blocker.tsx" switcher
01097| 'use client'
01098| 
01099| import { createContext, useState, useContext } from 'react'
01100| 
01101| interface NavigationBlockerContextType {
01102|   isBlocked: boolean
01103|   setIsBlocked: (isBlocked: boolean) => void
01104| }
01105| 
01106| export const NavigationBlockerContext =
01107|   createContext<NavigationBlockerContextType>({
01108|     isBlocked: false,
01109|     setIsBlocked: () => {},
01110|   })
01111| 
01112| export function NavigationBlockerProvider({
01113|   children,
01114| }: {
01115|   children: React.ReactNode
01116| }) {
01117|   const [isBlocked, setIsBlocked] = useState(false)
01118| 
01119|   return (
01120|     <NavigationBlockerContext.Provider value={{ isBlocked, setIsBlocked }}>
01121|       {children}
01122|     </NavigationBlockerContext.Provider>
01123|   )
01124| }
01125| 
01126| export function useNavigationBlocker() {
01127|   return useContext(NavigationBlockerContext)
01128| }
01129| ```
01130| 
01131| ```jsx filename="app/contexts/navigation-blocker.js" switcher
01132| 'use client'
01133| 
01134| import { createContext, useState, useContext } from 'react'
01135| 
01136| export const NavigationBlockerContext = createContext({
01137|   isBlocked: false,
01138|   setIsBlocked: () => {},
01139| })
01140| 
01141| export function NavigationBlockerProvider({ children }) {
01142|   const [isBlocked, setIsBlocked] = useState(false)
01143| 
01144|   return (
01145|     <NavigationBlockerContext.Provider value={{ isBlocked, setIsBlocked }}>
01146|       {children}
01147|     </NavigationBlockerContext.Provider>
01148|   )
01149| }
01150| 
01151| export function useNavigationBlocker() {

01155|

01158| ```tsx filename="app/components/form.tsx" switcher

01163| export default function Form() {
01164|   const { setIsBlocked } = useNavigationBlocker()
01165| 
01166|   return (
01167|     <form
01168|       onSubmit={(e) => {
01169|         e.preventDefault()
01170|         setIsBlocked(false)
01171|       }}
01172|       onChange={() => setIsBlocked(true)}
01173|     >
01174|       <input type="text" name="name" />
01175|       <button type="submit">Save</button>
01176|     </form>
01177|   )
01178| }
01179| ```
01180| 
01181| ```jsx filename="app/components/form.js" switcher
01182| 'use client'
01183| 
01184| import { useNavigationBlocker } from '../contexts/navigation-blocker'
01185| 
01186| export default function Form() {
01187|   const { setIsBlocked } = useNavigationBlocker()
01188| 
01189|   return (
01190|     <form
01191|       onSubmit={(e) => {
01192|         e.preventDefault()
01193|         setIsBlocked(false)
01194|       }}
01195|       onChange={() => setIsBlocked(true)}
01196|     >
01197|       <input type="text" name="name" />
01198|       <button type="submit">Save</button>
01199|     </form>
01200|   )
01201| }
01202| ```
01203| 
01204| Create a custom Link component that blocks navigation:
01205| 
01206| ```tsx filename="app/components/custom-link.tsx" switcher
01207| 'use client'
01208| 
01209| import Link from 'next/link'
01210| import { useNavigationBlocker } from '../contexts/navigation-blocker'
01211| 
01212| interface CustomLinkProps extends React.ComponentProps<typeof Link> {
01213|   children: React.ReactNode
01214| }
01215| 
01216| export function CustomLink({ children, ...props }: CustomLinkProps) {
01217|   const { isBlocked } = useNavigationBlocker()
01218| 
01219|   return (
01220|     <Link
01221|       onNavigate={(e) => {
01222|         if (
01223|           isBlocked &&
01224|           !window.confirm('You have unsaved changes. Leave anyway?')
01225|         ) {
01226|           e.preventDefault()
01227|         }
01228|       }}
01229|       {...props}
01230|     >
01231|       {children}
01232|     </Link>
01233|   )
01234| }
01235| ```
01236| 
01237| ```jsx filename="app/components/custom-link.js" switcher

01239|

---
title: Link Component
description: Enable fast client-side navigation with the built-in `next/link` component.
---

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

/**
 * OpenCode in-sandbox runner.
 *
 * This file is shipped INTO the sandbox by the orchestrator and executed there as
 * `node __agent_eval__/run.mjs '<AgentRunInput JSON>'`. It is intentionally
 * ZERO-DEPENDENCY (only `node:*` builtins) because the sandbox only has the
 * fixture's own deps + the installed `opencode` CLI — it cannot import anything
 * from the @vercel/agent-eval package.
 *
 * Dual mode:
 *   - runnable: invoked directly → reads argv, runs the agent, writes the result
 *     file + prints a status line, exits 0.
 *   - importable: `import { runAgent } from './run.mjs'` → returns a RunnerResult
 *     (no file write, no exit). This is what a future in-sandbox judge reuses.
 *
 * The pure helpers below are exported (not just `runAgent`) so they can be
 * unit-tested directly — the same code the sandbox runs (see opencode.test.ts).
 */

import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';

events.content:
Done. View transitions added following Next.js 16's `view-transitions` guide (read from `node_modules/next/dist/docs/`). Typecheck and `next build` both pass.

**What changed:**

- **Shared element morph** (`app/ProductGrid.tsx:14`, `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:53`) — both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero are wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`. The matching `name` makes the browser morph size/position between the two pages; `default="none"` keeps the pair from crossfading on unrelated transitions.

- **Directional slides** — grid `<Link>`s use `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`, the back link uses `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`. Both `page.tsx` files wrap their content in a per-type `<ViewTransition enter/exit={{'nav-forward'…, 'nav-back'…, default:'none'}}>`. CSS in `globals.css` slides forward content left / back content right (60px, asymmetric fade). Wrappers live in `page.tsx` (not the layout) since layouts persist and never exit/enter.

- **Suspense reveal** (`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx:62`) — the `DetailsSkeleton` fallback gets `exit="slide-down"` and `ProductDetails` gets `enter="slide-up"` (both `default="none"`), so the skeleton slides down/fades out and content slides up/fades in with staggered timing. Applied only to the actually-suspending boundary so it never fights the directional slide.

- **Reduced motion** (`app/globals.css`) — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` zeroes all `::view-transition-*` durations/delays and disables the skeleton `pulse` animation.

- **`::view-transition { pointer-events: none }`** keeps the page clickable mid-transition.

Note: `next build` auto-reformatted `tsconfig.json` (prettified + added `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts`) — a standard Next.js-managed change, left as-is.
